problem: Prior quadruped-robot learning handles vision-only policies (goal-image or terrain-perception, 'QUAR-VA', e.g. ViNT-style) and language-only policies (e.g. SayTap, 'QUAR-LA') separately. Vision-only policies cannot express fine-grained or compositional commands, and language-only policies cannot perceive the environment. No large-scale quadruped dataset pairing egocentric vision, language instructions and robot commands exists, and no suitable VLA action space has been defined for agile legged robots.
motivation: VLA models (RT-1/RT-2 style) merge perception, planning and decision-making, but so far only for fixed-base manipulators or 2-D mobile navigation. Legged robots need an action space that is richer than base velocities (gait, posture) yet slow enough for a large model to produce. Real-robot data is expensive, so the authors bet on massive, cheaply scripted simulation data co-trained with a small real set.
key_idea: Fine-tune a pretrained multimodal LLM (Fuyu-8B) to map one egocentric RGB image plus a language instruction to autoregressively generated, 256-bin-discretized tokens of an 11-D high-level quadruped command (velocity, gait, body posture) plus a terminate flag. A pretrained low-level locomotion policy executes these commands. Training uses a new large sim + small real multi-task dataset (QUARD).
insight: The ablation in supp. Table 'Detailed performance on different architecture' is the key lesson. Frozen-feature VLM + policy-head baselines reach 0 on Crawl and Unload, whether the head is an MLP (CLIP, VC-1) or an RT-1-style transformer. These tasks require coordinated changes of body height, pitch and foot parameters, not just x-velocity and yaw. Decoding action dimensions autoregressively through the full MLLM lets each dimension condition on the ones already decoded (Crawl SR 0.32 with Fuyu, 0.18 with LLaVA); the Fuyu vs LLaVA-7B swap changes results only moderately, so the authors credit the VLA paradigm rather than the specific backbone. Two further findings: multi-task co-training beats per-task training on every skill except the easiest one (QUART-Single 0.36 vs 0.60 on Go-to, 0.19 vs 0.53 on Go-avoid), and adding simulated data scales real-world success on Go-to from 3/20 (real only) to 7/20 (25.6K sim) to 13/20 (256K sim).
method: Task formulation (QUAR-VLA): a policy μ maps a single egocentric RGB image s and an instruction w to a 12-D action: [v_x, v_y, ω_z, gait phases θ1-θ3, stepping frequency f, body height h_z, pitch φ, foot width s_y, foot swing height h_z^f, terminate t].

Action tokenization: each continuous dimension is discretized into 256 uniform bins (following RT-1). Bins are mapped onto Fuyu's existing integer tokens ('symbol tuning'), and generated tokens are detokenized back to continuous commands (except the discrete terminate flag).

QUART model: Fuyu-8B, a decoder-only MLLM that encodes raw image patches, fine-tuned with next-token cross-entropy (behavior cloning) under causal masking. Training uses lr 2e-5, batch 256 and 100K steps. It generates the full action token sequence at about 2 Hz; a LLaVA-7B variant is also tested.

Hierarchical execution: the high-level commands are sent to a pretrained command-conditioned low-level locomotion controller (Margolis et al., Walk-These-Ways style), which produces the 12 joint actions at high frequency. This relaxes the control-rate demand on the large model.

QUARD dataset (sim): Isaac Gym massively parallel collection. Paths come from A* (D* in early collection, dropped because its sharp turns lose the target from view) using simulator ground-truth positions, and a PD controller converts paths to velocities at three speed levels and several gaits. Instructions follow templates. Six sim skills span three difficulty levels: distinguish letter, go to object, go through tunnel, go-to-and-avoid obstacle, crawl under bar, and unload a ball carried on the back into a receptacle. Targets are placed about 3 m ahead (x∈[2.7,3.3] m, y∈[0.9,1.1] m).

QUARD real + sim-real co-training: 3K teleoperated real 'go to object' episodes recorded with a front RealSense D435 camera are mixed with the large simulated set. Real performance is studied as the sim:real ratio is scaled (0K, 25.6K, 256K sim : 3K real).

setting.backbone: Fuyu-8B MLLM (fine-tuned end-to-end); LLaVA-7B variant in supplementary
setting.training_data: QUARD: large-scale Isaac Gym simulated demonstrations from scripted A*/D* + PD experts, about 256K-259K episodes (paper states 259K total; per-task table lists 10K distinguish, 72K go-to, 48K tunnel, 63K go-avoid, 1K crawl, 52K unload), plus 3K real-world teleoperated go-to-object episodes. Instructions are template language covering task, object, speed and gait.
setting.observation: single egocentric monocular RGB image (front RealSense D435 on the real robot) + language instruction; no proprioception at inference
setting.action_space: 11-D high-level locomotion commands (v_x, v_y, ω_z, 3 gait phase params, step frequency, body height, pitch, foot width, foot swing height) + terminate, each discretized into 256 bins as tokens, output at about 2 Hz and tracked by a pretrained low-level joint controller
setting.privileged: none at test time (simulator GT positions used only by the A*/D* expert for data collection)

numbers_note: The LaTeX source contains unfinished draft tables. 'holdouttasks' carries the caption 'the results has not to be added'. The 'seen' table (QUART-1 vs QUART-2) is marked 'need to be added'. The 'Inference speed' table is incomplete, and its CLIP row copies the overall-performance numbers. Table 'tab:sr' reports QUART-1 / QUART-2 at sim:real ratios 1:1 / 1:10 / 1:100, with averages 0.43/0.59/0.68 and 0.58/0.69/0.74. These QUART-1/QUART-2 variants are never defined in the text, so they are excluded. Internal inconsistencies: the per-task sim episode counts sum to 246K, while the text says 259K and the scaling table says 256K. 'Over 1500 episodes' is stated, but the listed per-task counts sum to 1350. The main-table Go-to SR (0.60) does not obviously match the per-object detailed table (0.72 / 0.60 / 0.64 / 0.44). Real-robot results beyond the 20-trial Go-to scaling study are only on the project website. Customized-skill results (spatial and compositional commands) are shown only qualitatively in figures. QUARD is a custom benchmark with no official splits: 'val-seen' / 'val-unseen' are assigned here to its seen and unseen evaluations, and 'test' to the real-robot trials.
results: On QUARD seen tasks in simulation, QUART (Fuyu-8B) beats the strongest baseline, VC-1 + language embedding + MLP head, on every skill: Distinguish 0.66 vs 0.46, Go-to 0.60 vs 0.43, Go-avoid 0.53 vs 0.45, Go-through 0.41 vs 0.31, Crawl 0.32 vs 0, Unload 0.12 vs 0. It also leads on unseen objects (0.35 vs 0.29) and paraphrased instructions (0.33 vs 0.19 for VC-1, 0.14 for CLIP). On the real robot, co-training with 256K simulated episodes raises Go-to success from 3/20 (real-only) to 13/20. Absolute success on hard whole-body skills remains low (Unload 0.12).
limitations: Toy, short-horizon settings: flat terrain, simple visually sparse scenes, targets about 3 m away, template language, and single-image input with no memory or proprioception. Real-robot evaluation is tiny (20 Go-to trials).
Slow 2 Hz inference and sim-to-real handled only by naive co-training; the authors acknowledge a persisting sim2real gap and inefficient data collection.

Evaluation quality is weak. The benchmark is self-made, baselines are frozen-feature encoders with MLP heads rather than other VLAs, and the draft contains undefined variants plus inconsistent dataset and episode counts across tables.
builds_on: Walk These Ways (Margolis et al. low-level command-conditioned locomotion policy)
compares_to: RT-1-style aligned VLM + transformer policy head
